1: # Bundled format blueprints
2: 
3: This directory contains the output-format blueprints that ship with this repo, so a fresh deployment
4: can write a doc or build a deck without anyone having to build one first. A *format* is an ordinary
5: blueprint the deployment has promoted (see `AdminConfig.formats`); these are the ones it promotes out
6: of the box.
7: 
8: Each `.gadget` file here is committed **as data**. The first `/api` request a deployment serves
9: installs them into the BLUEPRINTS KV namespace and BLUEPRINT_CONTENT R2 bucket (see
10: `src/format-blueprints.ts`), after which they are ordinary blueprints. Nothing wakes on deploy, so a
11: fresh deployment is provisioned by its first visitor.
12: 
13: ## Who owns what
14: 
15: A blueprint is two files with the same stem:
16: 
17: | | lives in | why |
18: | --- | --- | --- |
19: | the code, and the `bindings` it needs | `<name>.gadget` | what the blueprint *does* |
20: | `blueprintId`, title, description, `output` (noun/plural/icon), author, `revision` | `<name>.json` | what a human *curates*, so it's text in a reviewable file rather than fields inside a binary |
21: 
22: The installer writes the sidecar's values over whatever the archive happens to carry,
23: so an archive's own title and author are inert. The import script normalizes them anyway,
24: so the committed bytes don't contradict the sidecar.
25: 
26: ## Changing a title, description or author
27: 
28: Edit the sidecar and rebuild. That's all — no archive rewrite, no `revision` bump: everything that
29: ends up in the installed metadata is part of the installed-version fingerprint (see
30: `formatBlueprintsManifestVersion`), so a reinstall follows on the next deploy.
31: 
32: ## Updating a blueprint's code
33: 
34: Build it in a real Workshop, export it, and import the export:
35: 
36: ```
37: pnpm import:format-blueprint ~/Downloads/Gadgets-Doc-v4.gadget format.document
38: ```
39: 
40: That rewrites the archive, bumps `revision` in the sidecar, rebuilds
41: `src/generated/format-blueprints.ts`, and reports what it did:
42: 
43: ```
44: Updated workspace-docs.gadget (format.document)
45:   code         23668 -> 24489 bytes (7c5413e5a482)
46:   bindings     (none)
47:   version      3 -> 4
48:   revision     2 -> 3  (workspace-docs.json)
49: 
50:   presented as "Workspace Docs" by Cloudflare, from workspace-docs.json
51:                [export called it "Gadgets Doc"]
52: ```
53: 
54: The line worth reading is **`bindings`**, flagged `[CHANGED]` when the export needs something the old
55: copy didn't — an instantiating user will now be asked for it. `revision` is the reinstall trigger for
56: the one input the fingerprint can't see, the archive bytes; it's automated because forgetting it is
57: invisible (everything builds and deploys, and the old blueprint quietly stays put).
58: 
59: The script also round-trips the bytes it just wrote and checks the metadata and a content hash,
60: because these are committed as data and a corrupt archive would otherwise first surface when a
61: deployment tried to install it.
62: 
63: ## Adding a new format
64: 
65: `--new` writes the sidecar for you, filling in what it can from the export:
66: 
67: ```
68: pnpm import:format-blueprint ~/Downloads/Brief.gadget --new acme-brief
69: ```
70: 
71: It then prints the handful of fields worth editing before you deploy — chiefly `output`, the noun,
72: plural and icon the sidecar owns rather than the archive, and `output.id`, the grouping key on the
73: Outputs page.
74: Make that one **generic** (`document`, not `acme-brief`): the Outputs page groups by it, so a
75: "Contract" blueprint declaring `document` is listed with the rest of the documents instead of
76: adding a filter chip of its own.
77: 
78: `blueprintId` defaults to the name you passed. It is the install key: reimporting the same id
79: updates that blueprint in place, and **changing it after a deployment has installed it** promotes
80: the new id as a *second* format while the old one stays in the New menu, updated by nothing.
81: Rename files freely; the id is the load-bearing part.
82: 
83: 
84: ## Shipping your own formats
85: 
86: This directory is only the **default**. `FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS_DIR` points the build somewhere else:
87: 
88: ```
89: FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS_DIR=../../acme-formats pnpm exec vp run build
90: ```
91: 
92: `vp run`, not `pnpm build`: this package's `build` is a Vite+ task rather than a package.json
93: script, so pnpm cannot see it. `../vite.config.ts` explains why it has to be one.
94: 
95: Whatever directory it names *is* the deployment's format set — it replaces this one rather than
96: adding to it. Keep it in your own tree, in the same `<name>.gadget` + `<name>.json` layout; nothing
97: in it refers back to this repo. If you want one of ours too, copy the pair across once and own it
98: from then on.
99: 
100: This matters because this repo is usually a submodule: adding or deleting files *here* would
101: conflict on every update. Pointing the build at your own directory touches nothing, so the submodule
102: stays pristine forever. The import script honours the same variable, so you get the same workflow.
103: 
104: Two lighter options need no build change at all:
105: 
106: 1. **Promote your own blueprints.** These are ordinary blueprints, and the standard set is admin

display.text:
# Bundled format blueprints

This directory contains the output-format blueprints that ship with this repo, so a fresh deployment
can write a doc or build a deck without anyone having to build one first. A *format* is an ordinary
blueprint the deployment has promoted (see `AdminConfig.formats`); these are the ones it promotes out
of the box.

Each `.gadget` file here is committed **as data**. The first `/api` request a deployment serves
installs them into the BLUEPRINTS KV namespace and BLUEPRINT_CONTENT R2 bucket (see
`src/format-blueprints.ts`), after which they are ordinary blueprints. Nothing wakes on deploy, so a
fresh deployment is provisioned by its first visitor.

## Who owns what

A blueprint is two files with the same stem:

| | lives in | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the code, and the `bindings` it needs | `<name>.gadget` | what the blueprint *does* |
| `blueprintId`, title, description, `output` (noun/plural/icon), author, `revision` | `<name>.json` | what a human *curates*, so it's text in a reviewable file rather than fields inside a binary |

The installer writes the sidecar's values over whatever the archive happens to carry,
so an archive's own title and author are inert. The import script normalizes them anyway,
so the committed bytes don't contradict the sidecar.

## Changing a title, description or author

Edit the sidecar and rebuild. That's all — no archive rewrite, no `revision` bump: everything that
ends up in the installed metadata is part of the installed-version fingerprint (see
`formatBlueprintsManifestVersion`), so a reinstall follows on the next deploy.

## Updating a blueprint's code

Build it in a real Workshop, export it, and import the export:

```
pnpm import:format-blueprint ~/Downloads/Gadgets-Doc-v4.gadget format.document
```

That rewrites the archive, bumps `revision` in the sidecar, rebuilds
`src/generated/format-blueprints.ts`, and reports what it did:

```
Updated workspace-docs.gadget (format.document)
  code         23668 -> 24489 bytes (7c5413e5a482)
  bindings     (none)
  version      3 -> 4
  revision     2 -> 3  (workspace-docs.json)

  presented as "Workspace Docs" by Cloudflare, from workspace-docs.json
               [export called it "Gadgets Doc"]
```

The line worth reading is **`bindings`**, flagged `[CHANGED]` when the export needs something the old
copy didn't — an instantiating user will now be asked for it. `revision` is the reinstall trigger for
the one input the fingerprint can't see, the archive bytes; it's automated because forgetting it is
invisible (everything builds and deploys, and the old blueprint quietly stays put).

The script also round-trips the bytes it just wrote and checks the metadata and a content hash,
because these are committed as data and a corrupt archive would otherwise first surface when a
deployment tried to install it.

## Adding a new format

`--new` writes the sidecar for you, filling in what it can from the export:

```
pnpm import:format-blueprint ~/Downloads/Brief.gadget --new acme-brief
```

It then prints the handful of fields worth editing before you deploy — chiefly `output`, the noun,
plural and icon the sidecar owns rather than the archive, and `output.id`, the grouping key on the
Outputs page.
Make that one **generic** (`document`, not `acme-brief`): the Outputs page groups by it, so a
"Contract" blueprint declaring `document` is listed with the rest of the documents instead of
adding a filter chip of its own.

`blueprintId` defaults to the name you passed. It is the install key: reimporting the same id
updates that blueprint in place, and **changing it after a deployment has installed it** promotes
the new id as a *second* format while the old one stays in the New menu, updated by nothing.
Rename files freely; the id is the load-bearing part.


## Shipping your own formats

This directory is only the **default**. `FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS_DIR` points the build somewhere else:

```
FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS_DIR=../../acme-formats pnpm exec vp run build
```

`vp run`, not `pnpm build`: this package's `build` is a Vite+ task rather than a package.json
script, so pnpm cannot see it. `../vite.config.ts` explains why it has to be one.

Whatever directory it names *is* the deployment's format set — it replaces this one rather than
adding to it. Keep it in your own tree, in the same `<name>.gadget` + `<name>.json` layout; nothing
in it refers back to this repo. If you want one of ours too, copy the pair across once and own it
from then on.

This matters because this repo is usually a submodule: adding or deleting files *here* would
conflict on every update. Pointing the build at your own directory touches nothing, so the submodule
stays pristine forever. The import script honours the same variable, so you get the same workflow.

Two lighter options need no build change at all:

1. **Promote your own blueprints.** These are ordinary blueprints, and the standard set is admin
   curation (`AdminConfig.formats`). Publish a blueprint in your deployment and promote it in the
   admin Formats panel; disable the bundled ones you don't want. Nothing needs rebuilding, and this
   is the mechanism the bundled set is a convenience on top of, not a special case beside.
2. **Ship no formats.** Point `FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS_DIR` at an empty directory, and the deployment
   simply has none until an admin promotes something.

1: // Built-in WebFetch capability for the agent.
2: //
3: // Provides an HTTP GET against arbitrary public HTTPS URLs. There is intentionally no
4: // support for POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH or for forwarding credentials.
5: //
6: // Document-to-Markdown conversion is delegated to Cloudflare Workers AI's
7: // `env.WORKERS_AI.toMarkdown()` utility, which handles HTML, PDF, DOCX, XLSX/XLS, ODT/ODS,
8: // CSV, XML, and Apple Numbers documents. Image conversion is intentionally NOT exposed here
9: // because it uses paid Workers AI models. Plain-text, JSON, and other unknown content types
10: // pass through unconverted.
11: //
12: // SSRF protection: relies on workerd's post-DNS-lookup IP address filtering. The
13: // `global_fetch_strictly_public` compatibility flag (set in wrangler.jsonc) restricts
14: // `fetch()` to public IP addresses; reserved ranges (loopback, RFC1918, link-local,
15: // cloud-metadata, etc.) are rejected by the runtime, *after* the hostname has been
16: // resolved. This is the only correct place to enforce such restrictions, since a symbolic
17: // hostname can resolve to anything. `wrangler dev` reconfigures its global outbound to
18: // permit fetching from any address (so localhost services stay reachable), so the flag
19: // only takes effect in production -- an acceptable tradeoff for dev.
20: 
21: import type { AiGatewayConfig } from "./ai-gateway";
22: 
23: /**
24:  * The bits of the Workers AI binding and gateway config that `webFetch` needs. Kept narrow
25:  * so the caller can pass a stub in tests without constructing a full Cloudflare.Env.
26:  */
27: export type WebFetchEnv = {
28:   ai: Ai;
29:   gateway: AiGatewayConfig | null;
30: };
31: 
32: export type WebFetchInput = {
33:   url: string;
34:   /**
35:    * If true, return the exact response bytes (decoded as UTF-8) without any document
36:    * conversion. If false or omitted, supported document formats (HTML, PDF, DOCX, ...) are
37:    * converted to Markdown via env.WORKERS_AI.toMarkdown().
38:    */
39:   raw?: boolean;
40:   /** Caller-requested cap on body length (characters). Server enforces its own hard cap on top. */
41:   maxBytes?: number;
42: };
43: 
44: export type WebFetchResult = {
45:   status: number;
46:   finalUrl: string;
47:   contentType: string;
48:   body: string;
49:   truncated: boolean;
50: };
51: 
52: // Hard server-side limits.
53: const HARD_MAX_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024;     // 5 MiB after which we always truncate
54: const DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024;  // 1 MiB default cap when caller didn't specify
55: const FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 30_000;
56: const USER_AGENT = "GadgetsWebFetch/1.0";
57: 
58: /**
59:  * Validate a URL string for use with webFetch. Throws on bad input. Returns the parsed URL
60:  * on success.
61:  *
62:  * Note: we do NOT inspect the hostname for "looks-internal" patterns here. That kind of
63:  * blocklist is fundamentally unsound because a symbolic hostname can resolve to any IP at
64:  * fetch time. SSRF protection is provided post-DNS-lookup by workerd (see the file header).
65:  */
66: export function validateWebFetchUrl(input: string): URL {
67:   let parsed: URL;
68:   try {
69:     parsed = new URL(input);
70:   } catch {
71:     throw new Error(`Invalid URL: ${input}`);
72:   }
73: 
74:   if (parsed.protocol !== "https:") {
75:     throw new Error(
76:       `Only https:// URLs are allowed; got ${parsed.protocol}//. ` +
77:         `Use the HTTPS version of this URL.`,
78:     );
79:   }
80: 
81:   if (parsed.username || parsed.password) {
82:     throw new Error("URLs with embedded credentials are not allowed.");
83:   }
84: 
85:   return parsed;
86: }
87: 
88: // Read up to `maxBytes` from the body of a response. Returns the raw bytes (so callers can
89: // hand them to either a text decoder or a Blob) and a flag indicating whether the stream
90: // was truncated.
91: async function readBodyCapped(
92:   response: Response,
93:   maxBytes: number,
94: ): Promise<{ bytes: Uint8Array; truncated: boolean }> {
95:   if (!response.body) {
96:     return { bytes: new Uint8Array(0), truncated: false };
97:   }
98: 
99:   const reader = response.body.getReader();
100:   const chunks: Uint8Array[] = [];
101:   let total = 0;
102:   let truncated = false;
103: 
104:   try {
105:     while (true) {
106:       const { value, done } = await reader.read();
107:       if (done) break;
108:       if (!value) continue;
109: 
110:       if (total + value.byteLength > maxBytes) {
111:         // Take a partial slice to fill the budget exactly, then stop.
112:         const remaining = maxBytes - total;
113:         if (remaining > 0) {
114:           chunks.push(value.subarray(0, remaining));
115:           total += remaining;
116:         }
117:         truncated = true;
118:         break;
119:       }
120: 
121:       chunks.push(value);
122:       total += value.byteLength;
123:     }
124:   } finally {
125:     // If we stopped early, cancel the rest of the stream to free server-side resources.
126:     if (truncated) {
127:       try {
128:         await reader.cancel();
129:       } catch {
130:         // Ignore.
131:       }
132:     }
133:     reader.releaseLock();
134:   }
135: 
136:   const combined = new Uint8Array(total);
137:   let offset = 0;
138:   for (const c of chunks) {
139:     combined.set(c, offset);
140:     offset += c.byteLength;
141:   }
142:   return { bytes: combined, truncated };
143: }
144: 
145: function decodeUtf8(bytes: Uint8Array): string {
146:   return new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: false, ignoreBOM: false }).decode(bytes);
147: }
148: 
149: // Strip parameters from a Content-Type header (e.g. `text/html; charset=utf-8` -> `text/html`).
150: function baseContentType(contentType: string): string {
151:   const i = contentType.indexOf(";");
152:   return (i >= 0 ? contentType.slice(0, i) : contentType).trim().toLowerCase();
153: }
154: 
155: // MIME types that `env.WORKERS_AI.toMarkdown()` can convert for free (no Workers AI model
156: // usage). Derived from the public list of supported formats:
157: // https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers-ai/features/markdown-conversion/supported-formats/
158: //
159: // Image MIME types are intentionally excluded -- image conversion uses paid Workers AI
160: // models (object detection + Gemma-3 for image-to-text), and we don't want webFetch to
161: // silently incur per-fetch costs.
162: const TO_MARKDOWN_MIME_TYPES = new Set([
163:   "text/html",
164:   "application/xhtml+xml",
165:   "application/pdf",
166:   "application/xml",
167:   "text/xml",
168:   "text/csv",
169:   // Office / OpenDocument
170:   "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document", // .docx
171:   "application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet",       // .xlsx
172:   "application/vnd.ms-excel",                                                // .xls
173:   "application/vnd.ms-excel.sheet.macroenabled.12",                          // .xlsm
174:   "application/vnd.ms-excel.sheet.binary.macroenabled.12",                   // .xlsb
175:   "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet",                          // .ods
176:   "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text",                                 // .odt
177:   "application/vnd.apple.numbers",                                           // .numbers
178: ]);
179: 
180: // `toMarkdown()` uses the Workers AI binding, and binding calls only reach gateways in the
181: // Worker's own account -- so apply the platform gateway only when AiGatewayConfig resolves it
182: // as same-account (CF_AI_GATEWAY_USE_BINDING=false marks it cross-account).
183: function buildGatewayOptions(
184:   gateway: AiGatewayConfig | null,
185: ): GatewayOptions | undefined {
186:   if (!gateway) return undefined;
187:   if (!gateway.sameAccountGateway) return undefined;
188:   return { id: gateway.sameAccountGateway, metadata: { tool: "webFetch", automated: true } };
189: }
190: 
191: // Attempt to convert a document to Markdown using the Workers AI binding. Returns the
192: // Markdown body on success, or null if the document's MIME type isn't in the supported
193: // allow-list. Throws (with a contextual error) if the conversion itself fails.
194: async function convertToMarkdown(
195:   env: WebFetchEnv,
196:   bytes: Uint8Array,
197:   contentType: string,
198:   url: URL,
199: ): Promise<string | null> {
200:   const mime = baseContentType(contentType);
201:   if (!TO_MARKDOWN_MIME_TYPES.has(mime)) {
202:     return null;
203:   }
204: 
205:   // Build a name from the URL path so toMarkdown's format detection has a hint.
206:   const pathBasename = url.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean).pop() || "document";
207: 
208:   const result = await env.ai.toMarkdown(
209:     {
210:       name: pathBasename,
211:       blob: new Blob([bytes], { type: mime }),
212:     },
213:     {
214:       gateway: buildGatewayOptions(env.gateway),
215:       conversionOptions: {
216:         // Resolve relative links against the page's own origin.
217:         html: {
218:           hostname: url.origin,
219:           // Skip per-image summarization (which would invoke paid Workers AI models). The
220:           // agent gets a Markdown skeleton with image alt text and src URLs, which is
221:           // sufficient for documentation-lookup use cases.
222:           images: { convert: false, convertOGImage: false },
223:         },
224:       },
225:     },
226:   );
227: 
228:   if (result.format === "error") {
229:     throw new Error(`Markdown conversion failed: ${result.error}`);
230:   }
231:   return result.data;
232: }
233: 
234: 
235: 
236: // Parse the Content-Signal response header (https://contentsignals.org/) and check whether
237: // a specific signal is present and set to "no". The header is a comma-separated list of
238: // key=value pairs, e.g. `ai-train=yes, search=yes, ai-input=no`.
239: function contentSignalDenies(response: Response, signal: string): boolean {
240:   const header = response.headers.get("content-signal");
241:   if (!header) return false;
242:   for (const part of header.split(",")) {
243:     const [key, value] = part.split("=").map((s) => s.trim().toLowerCase());
244:     if (key === signal && value === "no") return true;
245:   }
246:   return false;
247: }
248: 
249: /**
250:  * Format a `WebFetchResult` as a single string for the agent: a small YAML frontmatter
251:  * header followed by `---` then the body. This is friendlier to LLMs than a JSON-wrapped
252:  * object, since the body lives inline rather than as an escaped JSON string.
253:  */
254: export function formatWebFetchResult(result: WebFetchResult): string {
255:   const lines = [
256:     "---",
257:     `url: ${result.finalUrl}`,
258:     `status: ${result.status}`,
259:     `content-type: ${result.contentType || "(unspecified)"}`,
260:     `truncated: ${result.truncated}`,
261:     "---",
262:     "",
263:     result.body,
264:   ];
265:   return lines.join("\n");
266: }
267: 
268: export async function webFetch(
269:   env: WebFetchEnv,
270:   input: WebFetchInput,
271: ): Promise<WebFetchResult> {
272:   const parsed = validateWebFetchUrl(input.url);
273: 
274:   const requestedMax = input.maxBytes ?? DEFAULT_MAX_BYTES;
275:   const maxBytes = Math.min(
276:     Math.max(1, Math.floor(requestedMax)),
277:     HARD_MAX_BYTES,
278:   );
279: 
280:   const abortController = new AbortController();
281:   const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => abortController.abort(), FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS);
282: 
283:   let response: Response;
284:   try {
285:     response = await fetch(parsed.toString(), {
286:       method: "GET",
287:       redirect: "follow",
288:       headers: {
289:         "user-agent": USER_AGENT,
290:         "accept": "text/markdown,text/html;q=0.9,text/plain;q=0.9,application/json;q=0.9,application/xhtml+xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8",
291:       },
292:       signal: abortController.signal,
293:     });
294:   } catch (err) {
295:     if (
296:       err instanceof Error &&
297:       (err.name === "AbortError" || /abort/i.test(err.message))
298:     ) {
299:       throw new Error(`Fetch timed out after ${FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS}ms`, { cause: err });
300:     }
301:     throw err;
302:   } finally {
303:     clearTimeout(timeoutId);
304:   }
305: 
306:   // `response.url` is set by the runtime to the final URL after any redirects. Fall back
307:   // to the original URL if it happens to be empty.
308:   const finalUrl = response.url ? new URL(response.url) : parsed;
309:   const contentType = response.headers.get("content-type") ?? "";
310: 
311:   // Respect the Content-Signal header (https://contentsignals.org/). If the site
312:   // explicitly sets `ai-input=no`, we must not feed its content to the AI agent.
313:   if (contentSignalDenies(response, "ai-input")) {
314:     try {
315:       await response.body?.cancel();
316:     } catch {
317:       // Ignore.
318:     }
319:     throw new Error(
320:       `The site at ${finalUrl} sets Content-Signal: ai-input=no, indicating that ` +
321:         `it does not permit its content to be used as AI input.`,
322:     );
323:   }
324: 
325:   const { bytes, truncated } = await readBodyCapped(response, maxBytes);
326: 
327:   let body: string;
328:   if (input.raw) {
329:     body = decodeUtf8(bytes);
330:   } else {
331:     const md = await convertToMarkdown(env, bytes, contentType, finalUrl);
332:     body = md !== null ? md : decodeUtf8(bytes);
333:   }
334: 
335:   return {
336:     status: response.status,
337:     finalUrl: finalUrl.toString(),
338:     contentType,
339:     body,
340:     truncated,
341:   };
342: }

(End of file - total 342 lines)
</content>

332:   let sequence = projection[keepFrom]?.sequence;

336:   if (sequence === undefined || sequence <= compactedTo) {

359:   for (let i = messages.length - 1; i >= 0; --i) {
360:     let message = messages[i];

395:     } else if (message.type === "agentCallback") {

410:         }

413:     }
414:   }

417:   // and folded over the compacted span -- an epoch boundary (an epochBoundary merge, or a

1: // Retry and telemetry for Durable Object reset rejections.
2: //
3: // workerd attaches the flags natively in the calling Worker, so no message matching is needed
4: // (jsg/util.c++, decodeTunneledException). Two independent axes: `retryable`/`overloaded` come
5: // from the kj exception TYPE (DISCONNECTED/OVERLOADED) and describe THIS CALL — one type per
6: // hop, so one flag per hop; `durableObjectReset` is parsed from the tunneled description and
7: // describes THE OBJECT, whose incarnation died, poisoning every stub to it. Hence the production
8: // storage-timeout reset is `{remote, overloaded, durableObjectReset}` with no `retryable`: it was
9: // shedding load AND it died. The docs cover `retryable`/`overloaded`/`remote`, but not
10: // `durableObjectReset` or the `durableObjectId` we log:
11: // https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/error-handling/
12: //
13: // Local vitest-pool-workers aborts reject FLAGLESS (pinned by the "user-DO reset flags"
14: // integration test), so the predicates and the retry path are unit-tested with synthetic
15: // production shapes.
16: 
17: import { createWorkshopLogger } from "./observability";
18: 
19: const logger = createWorkshopLogger("workshop.server");
20: 
21: /**
22:  * True for rejections caused by a DO reset or lost connection. This is the telemetry
23:  * classification, deliberately not the retry policy, which is narrower (see
24:  * `shouldRetryAfterReset`): a bare `overloaded` is excluded here only because a live object
25:  * shedding load is not a reset.
26:  */
27: export function isDoResetError(e: unknown): boolean {
28:   if (typeof e !== "object" || e === null) return false;
29:   const flags = e as { durableObjectReset?: unknown; retryable?: unknown };
30:   return flags.durableObjectReset === true || flags.retryable === true;
31: }
32: 
33: /** Wraps a DO stub so every method call observes DO-reset rejections for telemetry
34:  * (`user_do.reset.surfaced`, with the method name as the operation) and rethrows them
35:  * unchanged. Otherwise transparent. Pass the caller's logger so the log attributes the reset
36:  * to the component (and context, e.g. gadgetId) that observed it; defaults to the Worker's.
37:  * A surfaced reset may still be absorbed by `retryOnDoReset` at the call site (correlate with
38:  * `user_do.reset.recovered`). */
39: export function wrapDoStubForTelemetry<T extends { id: DurableObjectId }>(
40:     stub: T, log: ReturnType<typeof createWorkshopLogger> = logger): T {
41:   return new Proxy(stub, {
42:     get(target, prop) {
43:       const value = Reflect.get(target, prop) as unknown;
44:       if (typeof value !== "function") return value;
45:       // Invoke through the stub (`target[prop](...)`) rather than `.apply` on the extracted
46:       // handle: native RPC method handles are themselves proxies, and touching `.apply` on one
47:       // is interpreted as a nested RPC property access (the DO then rejects a call to "apply").
48:       const methods = target as unknown as Record<PropertyKey, (...a: unknown[]) => unknown>;
49:       if (typeof prop !== "string") return (...args: unknown[]) => methods[prop](...args);
50:       return (...args: unknown[]) => {
51:         const result = methods[prop](...args);
52:         if (typeof (result as PromiseLike<unknown> | undefined)?.then !== "function") return result;
53:         return (async () => {
54:           try {
55:             return await (result as PromiseLike<unknown>);
56:           } catch (e) {
57:             if (isDoResetError(e)) {
58:               log.warn("user DO reset observed", {
59:                 event: "user_do.reset.surfaced",
60:                 operation: prop,
61:                 durableObjectId: target.id.toString(),
62:                 error: e,
63:               });
64:             }
65:             throw e;
66:           }
67:         })();
68:       };
69:     },
70:   });
71: }
72: 
73: // Full jitter decorrelates the replay burst a mass reset produces (a reset fails every
74: // in-flight call from every session at once); workerd queues the fresh-stub request behind
75: // the object restart, so no delay floor is needed.
76: const RETRY_JITTER_MS = 250;
77: 
78: /** Whether a rejection may be retried, given a call already known to be replay-safe.
79:  * Narrower than `isDoResetError`: `durableObjectReset` retries even with `overloaded` set (the
80:  * incarnation is dead — the queue that overloaded it died with it; this is the shape production
81:  * storage-timeout resets arrive in), a deliberate divergence from the never-retry-`overloaded`
82:  * guidance in the error-handling docs linked above. Bare `retryable` (connection lost to a
83:  * possibly-live object) retries only if it isn't shedding load. */
84: function shouldRetryAfterReset(e: unknown): boolean {
85:   if (typeof e !== "object" || e === null) return false;
86:   const flags = e as { durableObjectReset?: unknown; retryable?: unknown; overloaded?: unknown };
87:   if (flags.durableObjectReset === true) return true;
88:   return flags.retryable === true && flags.overloaded !== true;
89: }
90: 
91: /** Retries `callWithFreshStub` once if it rejects with a DO-reset shape. The caller asserts the
92:  * call is replay-safe (a reset can't distinguish "never applied" from "applied, response lost")
93:  * — wrap pure reads only. The thunk must mint its stub inside itself (e.g. via the fresh-stub
94:  * getters) so the second attempt gets a fresh incarnation; a captured stub is permanently broken
95:  * and retrying it is a silent no-op. Pass the same logger the stub's `wrapDoStubForTelemetry`
96:  * uses so the recovery is attributed to the component (and context, e.g. gadgetId) whose
97:  * surfaced warning it absorbs; defaults to the Worker's. */
98: export async function retryOnDoReset<T>(
99:     callWithFreshStub: () => Promise<T>,
100:     log: ReturnType<typeof createWorkshopLogger> = logger): Promise<T> {
101:   try {
102:     return await callWithFreshStub();
103:   } catch (e) {
104:     if (!shouldRetryAfterReset(e)) throw e;  // identity rethrow, flags intact
105:     await scheduler.wait(Math.random() * RETRY_JITTER_MS);
106:     let recovered = await callWithFreshStub();  // a second rejection propagates by identity
107:     log.info("recovered from user DO reset", { event: "user_do.reset.recovered" });
108:     return recovered;
109:   }
110: }

1: // Sign-in via authentication gatekeepers.
2: //
3: // Unlike the normal connect-account flow (which runs for an already-logged-in user), login happens
4: // before we know who the user is. The PublicApi starts a gatekeeper connect flow (in "auth" scope
5: // mode) with a `LoginConnectCallbackImpl` as the callback and a `PendingLogin` DO to bridge the
6: // result back to the waiting browser:
7: //
8: //   1. PublicApi.startGatekeeperLogin(vendorId) creates a PendingLogin DO (keyed by a random DO id),
9: //      hands the gatekeeper a LoginConnectCallbackImpl, and returns {url, attempt}, where `attempt`
10: //      is an RpcStub wrapping the DO (so the client awaits via a capability, never a guessable id).
11: //   2. The browser opens `url` (the gatekeeper's self-closing OAuth popup) and calls
12: //      `attempt.wait()`, which blocks on the PendingLogin DO.
13: //   3. When the gatekeeper finishes, it calls LoginConnectCallbackImpl.complete(user). We read the
14: //      verified email, resolve/create the email-keyed user DO, mint a session, and deliver the token
15: //      to the PendingLogin DO, which resolves the awaiting RPC.
16: //
17: // Sign-in only requests minimal scopes and the gatekeeper grant is transient (it self-destructs
18: // shortly after we read the email) — so login does NOT create a persistent connected account.
19: // Capability access (repos, docs, billing) is granted later when the user explicitly connects the
20: // gatekeeper, which requests the full scopes and persists the connection.
21: 
22: import { DurableObject, WorkerEntrypoint } from "cloudflare:workers";
23: import { GatekeeperConnectCallback, GatekeeperUser } from "@gadgets/workshop-shared/gatekeeper";
24: import { createWorkshopLogger } from "../observability";
25: import { CLOUDFLARE_VENDOR_ID } from "../user.js";
26: import { readAdminConfig } from "../admin-config.js";
27: 
28: const logger = createWorkshopLogger("workshop.auth");
29: 
30: type PendingResult = { token: string } | { error: string };
31: 
32: /**
33:  * Bridges a login result from the (separate) OAuth-callback invocation back to the waiting browser.
34:  *
35:  * This DO holds no durable storage: a login normally completes within seconds, and the in-flight
36:  * awaitResult() request keeps the DO alive so the in-memory waiter is reachable when deliver()/fail()
37:  * fire. If the attempt is abandoned, the client disposes the awaiting RPC (the `attempt` stub) and
38:  * the DO is simply evicted — no alarm or cleanup needed.
39:  */
40: export class PendingLogin extends DurableObject<Cloudflare.Env> {
41:   // Awaiters from in-flight awaitResult() calls, resolved/rejected when the result arrives.
42:   #waiters: { resolve: (token: string) => void; reject: (err: Error) => void }[] = [];
43:   // Stash for the rare case deliver()/fail() arrives before awaitResult() registers a waiter.
44:   #result?: PendingResult;
45: 
46:   /** Block until the login completes (or fails). */
47:   async awaitResult(): Promise<string> {
48:     if (this.#result) {
49:       const result = this.#result;
50:       this.#result = undefined;  // one-time use
51:       if ("token" in result) return result.token;
52:       throw new Error(result.error);
53:     }
54:     return await new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
55:       this.#waiters.push({ resolve, reject });
56:     });
57:   }
58: 
59:   /**
60:    * Called by LoginConnectCallbackImpl on success: resolve the awaiter (or stash the token if none
61:    * is waiting yet).
62:    */
63:   async deliver(token: string): Promise<void> {
64:     if (this.#waiters.length > 0) {
65:       for (const w of this.#waiters) w.resolve(token);
66:       this.#waiters = [];
67:     } else {
68:       this.#result = { token };
69:     }
70:   }
71: 
72:   async fail(reason: string): Promise<void> {
73:     if (this.#waiters.length > 0) {
74:       for (const w of this.#waiters) w.reject(new Error(reason));
75:       this.#waiters = [];
76:     } else {
77:       this.#result = { error: reason };
78:     }
79:   }
80: }
81: 
82: type LoginCallbackProps = { pendingId: string; vendorId: string };
83: 
84: export class LoginConnectCallbackImpl
85:     extends WorkerEntrypoint<Cloudflare.Env, LoginCallbackProps>
86:     implements GatekeeperConnectCallback {
87:   #pending() {
88:     const id = this.ctx.exports.PendingLogin.idFromString(this.ctx.props.pendingId);
89:     return this.ctx.exports.PendingLogin.get(id);
90:   }
91: 
92:   async complete(account: Fetcher<GatekeeperUser>, expiresAt?: Date): Promise<void> {
93:     const loginLogger = logger.with({
94:       operation: "gatekeeper.login",
95:       vendorId: this.ctx.props.vendorId,
96:     });
97:     const pending = this.#pending();
98:     // `account` is a call parameter, so Cap'n Web disposes it automatically when this method
99:     // returns — no explicit disposal needed. We read the verified email to resolve/create the user.
100:     // The email's local-part seeds the initial display name, like the Cloudflare Access flow.
101:     try {
102:       const email = await account.getAuthenticatedEmail();
103:       if (!email) {
104:         loginLogger.info("gatekeeper login finished", {
105:           event: "gatekeeper.login.finished", outcome: "no_email",
106:         });
107:         await pending.fail("This account has no verified email, so it can't be used to sign in.");
108:         return;
109:       }
110:       const userStub = this.ctx.exports.UserDurableObject.get(
111:           this.ctx.exports.UserDurableObject.idFromName(email));
112:       // Closed signups block first-time account creation here too (not just password signup); an
113:       // existing user signing in is unaffected.
114:       const signupsEnabled = (await readAdminConfig(this.env)).signupsEnabled;
115:       const secret = await userStub.loginOrCreateViaGatekeeper(email, signupsEnabled);
116:       if (secret === null) {
117:         loginLogger.info("gatekeeper login finished", {
118:           event: "gatekeeper.login.finished", outcome: "signups_disabled",
119:         });
120:         await pending.fail("New sign-ups are currently disabled on this deployment.");
121:         return;
122:       }
123:       // For Cloudflare, signing in also links the account for AI Gateway billing: startGatekeeperLogin
124:       // requested full (non-transient) scopes, so persist the grant as a connected account before
125:       // handing back the session. Other providers use minimal, transient sign-in grants (no persist).
126:       if (this.ctx.props.vendorId === CLOUDFLARE_VENDOR_ID) {
127:         await userStub.linkConnectedAccountFromLogin(account, this.ctx.props.vendorId, expiresAt);
128:       }
129:       // Session tokens are "<doName>:<secret>"; PublicApi.authenticate() routes via idFromName of
130:       // the first part. The user DO is keyed by email, so the prefix must be the email.
131:       await pending.deliver(`${email}:${secret}`);
132:       loginLogger.info("gatekeeper login finished", {
133:         event: "gatekeeper.login.finished", outcome: "ok",
134:       });
135:     } catch (err) {
136:       loginLogger.error("gatekeeper login failed", {
137:         event: "gatekeeper.login.failed", error: err,
138:       });
139:       loginLogger.info("gatekeeper login finished", {
140:         event: "gatekeeper.login.finished", outcome: "error",
141:       });
142:       await pending.fail("Sign-in failed. Please try again.");
143:     }
144:   }
145: 
146:   /**
147:    * No-ops: for transient sign-in grants there's nothing persisted to update. For the Cloudflare
148:    * billing connection (persisted on login) these would ideally flip the account's credential flag,
149:    * but the callback doesn't carry the user/account identity (it's only learned in complete()). The
150:    * billing path degrades gracefully regardless — getUsableAccessToken() returns null on expiry and
151:    * the user falls back to the free tier / a reconnect prompt.
152:    */
153:   async credentialsExpired(): Promise<void> {}
154:   async credentialsRestored(_expiresAt?: Date): Promise<void> {}
155: }
